unit.title: Functions as a Unifying Language
unit.act: Act XII - Organizing algebra around input and output
unit.role: Consolidate earlier relationships into function language without preempting full Precalculus theory.
unit.governingQuestion: How can one input-output framework organize the algebraic families already studied?
unit.storyArc: Relations become functions when each input has one output. Function notation separates evaluation from solving; domain and range collect restrictions and outputs; piecewise functions and arithmetic unify earlier examples.
outcomes: Determine whether a relation is a function.
Evaluate functions and solve output equations.
Determine domain and range from formulas, graphs, and contexts.
Interpret graph behavior and piecewise rules.
Combine functions arithmetically while tracking domain.
unit.investigation: Choose among linear, quadratic, rational, radical, and exponential models for unlabeled data or graphs.
unit.mastery: Students move among table, graph, formula, and context and distinguish evaluation from solving.

opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make relations and functions necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.

exposition: Define a function as exactly one output for each allowed input. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In relations and functions, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Mapping diagrams. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Discrete and continuous relations. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.
